data.kind: Spirometry report (pre and post salbutamol 400 micrograms)

script.opening: “Hiya. So the nurse did the blowing test. I’ve just got a smoker’s cough really — I need a stronger inhaler, don’t I? The blue one isn’t doing much.”

facts.text: “About two years. I get puffed going up the stairs at work — I have to stop halfway. I walk slower than my friends.”
“Every morning — white phlegm. Worse in winter.” No blood ever. No chest pain.
No weight loss, appetite fine, no night sweats, no ankle swelling.
No asthma as a child, no hay fever or eczema, no night-time waking with wheeze, no big day-to-day swings.
First says: “I’ve cut down.” If asked how many now: “...about twenty. I told the nurse less. I’m ashamed.” Started at 15. Tried patches once — “gave me nightmares”. Never tried a vape or medicine.
Night shifts at a care home — lifting, stairs. “I can’t afford to lose this job.”

facts.topic: Your mum (only if asked what you think it is or what worries you)
facts.text: “My mum had emphysema. She ended up on oxygen at home, couldn’t leave the house, died at 66. Is that what I’ve got?” Tearful.
Uses salbutamol 2–3 times a week. If asked to show technique: presses and breathes at the same time, no spacer, holds breath only briefly.
Had flu jab at work last year. Not sure about pneumonia jab.

Start upbeat and dismissive (“smoker’s cough”). Tell the smoking truth only if asked without judgement. When COPD is named, become worried and mention your mum. If the doctor explains that stopping smoking now changes the outlook and that your lungs are not like your mum’s at the end, you become motivated and accept the stop smoking referral. React badly to lecturing: “I know, I know.”

ice.ideas: “Just a smoker’s cough — I need a stronger inhaler.”
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — her mother died at 66 housebound on oxygen with emphysema and she fears the same; she is ashamed that she still smokes 20 a day despite saying she has cut down; she fears losing her job.

cues: “I’ve cut down.” — invites a kind, specific question.
“Is that what I’ve got?” (about her mum) — the fear.

checkpoints.text: Interprets the spirometry correctly: post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC 0.57 (obstruction), FEV1 68% predicted (moderate), minimal reversibility (80 mL) — consistent with COPD not asthma

Confirms the clinical picture (exertional breathlessness, productive cough, smoking history) and asks about asthmatic features and red flags (haemoptysis, weight loss, chest pain), using the CXR and FBC already done
Takes an accurate current smoking history non-judgementally and checks inhaler technique
Makes smoking cessation the priority: very brief advice, referral to stop smoking service, and options (combination NRT, varenicline, or a vape)
Inhaler plan: SABA with correct technique and spacer; explains next step (LABA+LAMA) if still breathless or exacerbating; not an inhaled steroid without asthmatic features
Refers to pulmonary rehabilitation (MRC 3), offers vaccinations, a self-management plan for exacerbations, and annual review
Explores and answers the fear about her mother: explains moderate COPD and that stopping smoking slows decline; addresses work concerns
Avoids lecturing; uses plain language; checks understanding and agrees follow-up

worked.txt: “The test measures how much air you can blow out and how fast. You can blow out a normal amount overall, but it comes out slowly — that’s what we call narrowing of the airways. The inhaler didn’t open it much, which tells us this is COPD rather than asthma.”
“Lots of people find it hard to cut down. Roughly how many a day are you smoking at the moment?”

“Your test shows moderate COPD — your lungs are working at about two-thirds of what we’d expect, not the stage your mum reached. The single biggest thing that slows it down is stopping smoking, and that’s still in your hands.”
“The best chance of stopping is support plus medication — that makes you about three times more likely to succeed than willpower alone. Can I refer you to the stop smoking service today?”
“A stronger inhaler won’t help much while the technique isn’t right. Let’s add a spacer and practise — and if you’re still breathless, there’s a two-in-one long-acting inhaler next.”
“Pulmonary rehab is an exercise and education course. People do better on it than on almost any inhaler — and it could help with the stairs at work.”

f.learning: COPD is diagnosed by symptoms and risk factors plus post-bronchodilator spirometry showing FEV1/FVC below 0.7; severity is graded by FEV1 % predicted (mild 80% or more with symptoms, moderate 50–79%, severe 30–49%, very severe under 30%). Large reversibility (over 400 mL) suggests asthma. Explain spirometry in plain language. NICE management: smoking cessation is the most effective intervention (offer behavioural support plus pharmacotherapy — combination NRT or varenicline — and e-cigarettes as an option); offer pneumococcal and annual flu vaccination (and COVID-19 as eligible); pulmonary rehabilitation for those functionally limited (MRC 3 or more, or 2 if limited); a personalised self-management plan; optimise treatable traits and comorbidities. Inhalers: SABA or SAMA first; if still limited and no asthmatic or steroid-responsive features, LABA+LAMA; consider LABA+ICS only with asthmatic features or raised eosinophils. Check technique before escalating. Address emotional responses (fear from a family history, shame about smoking) to support engagement.

knowledge.guideline: NICE NG115 Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease in over 16s: diagnosis and management (2018, updated 2019) · NICE NG209 Tobacco: preventing uptake, promoting quitting and treating dependence (2021) · NICE QS10 Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease in adults (quality standard; 2011, updated 2016)
knowledge.summary: Obstructive, non-reversible spirometry with symptoms and smoking = moderate COPD. Priority is stopping smoking; then technique, SABA, rehab, vaccines, self-management — and answering her fear.

points.t: Post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC 0.57 (below 0.7 and below LLN) = obstruction. FEV1 68% predicted = moderate. FVC preserved. Reversibility 80 mL (5%) = not significant; over 400 mL suggests asthma.

Chest X-ray (done) for alternative diagnoses and lung cancer features; FBC for anaemia or polycythaemia; BMI. Red flags: haemoptysis, weight loss, chest pain, hoarseness — consider suspected cancer pathway referral.

Very brief advice (ask, advise, act); referral to stop smoking service; combination NRT, varenicline or e-cigarettes. Behavioural support plus medicine roughly triples quit rates compared with unassisted attempts.

SABA or SAMA as required. If breathless or exacerbating despite this and no asthmatic features: LABA+LAMA. Asthmatic features or eosinophils supporting steroid responsiveness: consider LABA+ICS. Always check technique, adherence and smoking first.
Pulmonary rehabilitation (MRC 3 or more); flu and pneumococcal vaccines; self-management plan with rescue pack if appropriate; nutrition; anxiety and depression screening; annual review.
Moderate COPD; stopping smoking slows the decline of lung function to near that of a non-smoker. Oxygen is used only for chronic hypoxaemia, not breathlessness alone.
Pass: correct interpretation and plan. Clear pass: the truthful smoking history obtained without judgement, the mother’s story addressed, and a plan she is motivated to follow.

model.text: Hello Linda, I’m Dr Ali. I’ve got your breathing test results. Before we look at them, what did you make of the test?
Just a smoker’s cough. I need a stronger inhaler — the blue one isn’t doing much.
Let’s see what the test says and then sort the inhaler. Tell me about the breathing — what’s it stopping you doing?
Stairs at work, I stop halfway. Cough every morning with white phlegm.
Any blood in the phlegm, weight loss, chest pain? Any asthma, hay fever, or night-time wheeze?
No, none of that.
And smoking — lots of people find it hard to cut down. Roughly how many a day at the moment?
(pause) About twenty. I told the nurse less. I’m ashamed.
Thank you for telling me — that helps me help you. Could you show me how you use the blue inhaler?
(presses and breathes at the same time, short breath-hold)

The test shows you can blow out a normal amount of air, but it comes out slowly — your airways are narrowed. The inhaler didn’t open them much, so this is COPD, not asthma. It’s at a moderate level — your lungs work at about two-thirds of what we’d expect.
COPD? My mum had emphysema. She ended up on oxygen, stuck in the house. Is that me?
I’m sorry — that must have been hard to watch. You’re not where your mum was at the end. And the biggest thing that slows COPD down is stopping smoking — it’s still in your hands.
model.why: Addresses the fear and builds motivation

model.text: With support and medication, you’re around three times more likely to stop than on willpower. Would you like a referral to the stop smoking service today? Options include patches with a fast-acting spray or gum, varenicline tablets, or a vape.
model.why: Smoking cessation as priority with options

model.text: Yes. The patches gave me nightmares though.

Taking them off at night often helps, or varenicline might suit you. For the inhaler, let’s add a spacer — slow breath in, hold for ten. If you’re still breathless in a few weeks, the next step is a long-acting two-in-one inhaler.
model.why: Tailored cessation; technique before escalation; next step

model.text: I’d also like you to do pulmonary rehab — an exercise course that helps breathlessness more than most inhalers — and have the pneumonia jab and flu jab. The nurse will write you a plan for flare-ups.
Will I lose my job?

Many people keep working with COPD. If the stairs are a problem, a fit note can suggest adjustments while rehab helps. If you get a fever, more phlegm that turns green, or more breathlessness, contact us the same day; if you’re very breathless or have chest pain, call 999.
What will you take away from today?
It’s COPD, not as bad as Mum’s, stopping smoking is the main thing, spacer, rehab, jabs. And I’m not stuck yet.

social.t: Watching a parent die of COPD shapes beliefs; use it as motivation, not threat.
Physically demanding night shifts; rehab and adjustments can help keep her working.

legal.t: COPD may be a disability if it has a substantial long-term effect, triggering reasonable adjustments.

professional.t: Under-reported smoking is common; non-judgemental questions get accurate histories.

community.t: Local stop smoking service; pulmonary rehabilitation; Asthma + Lung UK Breathe Easy groups.

ice: Concern: ending up like her mum

playbook.diagnosis: COPD, moderate (post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC 0.57, FEV1 68% predicted, not reversible), MRC 3, current smoker 20/day.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Your airways are narrowed from smoking — a lung condition called COPD. It’s moderate, and stopping smoking is the best way to protect what you have.”

management.reflectIce: “You wanted a stronger inhaler and you’re frightened of ending up like your mum. Stopping smoking and rehab will do more than any inhaler.”
management.psychosocial: Address shame; work adjustments; family support for quitting.
sharedPlan: Stop smoking service referral; varenicline or combination NRT or vape
Spacer and technique; LABA+LAMA if still symptomatic
safetyNet: 999 for severe breathlessness or chest pain

pitfalls.intro: This station is failed by escalating inhalers on request, or by a smoking lecture that shuts her down.

items.fail: Prescribes a steroid-containing inhaler because she asked for something stronger.
items.why: Without asthmatic features ICS adds pneumonia risk; technique and smoking are the real issues.
items.fix: Check technique, add a spacer, and explain the LABA+LAMA step.

items.why: Shame increases concealment and reduces quit attempts.
items.fix: Ask kindly, praise honesty, offer support with medicine.

items.fail: Misreads the spirometry as asthma or as normal because FVC is normal.
items.why: The ratio defines obstruction; reversibility is minimal.
items.fix: Ratio first, FEV1 for severity, reversibility for asthma.

timeMap.d: Her idea: smoker’s cough, stronger inhaler.
Red flags, asthma features, true smoking, technique.
Spirometry in plain words; COPD moderate; her mum.
Stop smoking, technique and spacer, next inhaler step, rehab, vaccines, work.

wordPics.clearFail: Misinterprets the spirometry or gives an inhaled steroid on request; no smoking discussion or a lecture; red flags not checked.
wordPics.fail: Correct diagnosis but jargon-heavy explanation; smoking discussed without a concrete referral; mother’s story missed.
wordPics.pass: Interprets spirometry correctly, explains COPD, prioritises smoking cessation with referral, checks technique, offers rehab and vaccines.
wordPics.clearPass: All of the Pass, plus an honest smoking history obtained without judgement, the fear about her mother addressed with realistic hope, work concerns handled, and a motivated, specific plan.

avoid.instead: “The air comes out more slowly than it should.”

avoid.dont: “You have to stop smoking or you’ll end up like your mum.”
avoid.instead: “Stopping now is the biggest thing you can do to stay active.”
“Let’s get the technique right first, then step up if needed.”
avoid.why: Escalation without technique checks is ineffective.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Follows “just a smoker’s cough”, “I’ve cut down” and “is that what I’ve got?” about her mother.
Idea (smoker’s cough, needs a stronger inhaler); concern (her mother’s fate, shame about smoking, her job); expectation (a stronger inhaler).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — her mother died at 66 housebound on oxygen with emphysema and she fears the same; she is ashamed that she still smokes 20 a day despite saying she has cut down; she fears losing her job — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.
